claim: Distal contacts between nucleosomes over one kilobase from each other increase in quiescent cells compared to log phase cells.
source: We have previously shown that distal contacts between nucleosomes over one kilobase (kb) from each other increase in quiescent cells compared to log (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Swygert et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Swygert et al., 2019) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: In log phase cells, next neighbor (n+1) nucleosome interactions are strongly favored, with interactions sharply decreasing with increasing distance.
source: In log, next neighbor (n+1) interactions are strongly favored, with interactions sharply decreasing with increasing distance.
evidence: Supported by contact probability analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: In quiescent cells, short-range n+1 and n+2 contacts under 500 bp decrease to similar levels, and long-range interactions from 500 to 1000 bp are more frequent.
source: In contrast, in quiescent cells, short-range n+1 and n+2 contacts under 500 bp decrease to similar levels, and long-range interactions from 500 to 1000 bp are more frequent.
evidence: Supported by contact probability analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: The increase in long-range contacts in quiescent cells is consistent with a locally folded chromatin fiber.
source: This increase in long-range contacts in quiescent cells is consistent with a locally folded chromatin fiber.
evidence: Inference drawn from the contact probability data

claim: Even relatively highly expressed genes in quiescent cells display an increase in the distance of long-range nucleosome contacts as compared to log.
source: This analysis revealed that even relatively highly expressed genes in quiescent cells display an increase in the distance of long-range nucleosome contacts as compared to log, suggesting the increase in long-range contacts is not a consequence of transcriptional repression but instead a genome-wide change in nucleosome contact pattern.
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of Pol II ChIP-seq data and Micro-C contact maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C)

claim: The increase in long-range contacts is not a consequence of transcriptional repression but instead a genome-wide change in nucleosome contact pattern.
source: This analysis revealed that even relatively highly expressed genes in quiescent cells display an increase in the distance of long-range nucleosome contacts as compared to log, suggesting the increase in long-range contacts is not a consequence of transcriptional repression but instead a genome-wide change in nucleosome contact pattern.
evidence: Inference based on analysis of expressed genes showing similar long-range contact patterns

claim: Omitting DSG only subtly affected Micro-C XL results in quiescent cells.
source: Omitting DSG only subtly affected Micro-C XL results in quiescent cells, with 200 bp resolution (Figure 1B), genome-wide (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), and 1 kb resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) Micro-C XL heatmaps all appearing very similar.
evidence: Supported by comparison of Micro-C XL data with and without DSG shown in figures

claim: The HiCRep stratum-adjusted correlation coefficient (SCC) calculated between quiescent cell Micro-C samples with and without DSG was 0.95.
source: Consistently, the HiCRep stratum-adjusted correlation coefficient (SCC) calculated between quiescent cell Micro-C samples with and without DSG was 0.95 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), the same as between biological replicates performed the same way (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Quantitative measurement using HiCRep method

claim: Omitting DSG from Micro-C XL of log cells diminished long-range interactions.
source: In striking contrast, omitting DSG from Micro-C XL of log cells diminished long-range interactions (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D), and the SCC between data with and without DSG was 0.82 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by Micro-C XL data comparison and SCC calculation

claim: The SCC between log cell Micro-C data with and without DSG was 0.82.
source: In striking contrast, omitting DSG from Micro-C XL of log cells diminished long-range interactions (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D), and the SCC between data with and without DSG was 0.82 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement using HiCRep method

claim: Use of long crosslinkers disproportionately captures longer-range and/or more transient local inter-nucleosomal interactions in log cells.
source: This suggests that use of long crosslinkers disproportionately captures longer-range and/or more transient local inter-nucleosomal interactions in log cells, consistent with a less folded and more dynamic chromatin fiber in log versus quiescent cells.
evidence: Inference based on differential effects of DSG omission between log and quiescent cells

claim: Log cells have a less folded and more dynamic chromatin fiber compared to quiescent cells.
source: This suggests that use of long crosslinkers disproportionately captures longer-range and/or more transient local inter-nucleosomal interactions in log cells, consistent with a less folded and more dynamic chromatin fiber in log versus quiescent cells.
evidence: Inference based on crosslinker dependency of inter-nucleosomal interactions

claim: Inter-nucleosomal contacts in log cells occur at much lower distance than in quiescent cells.
source: Additionally, genome-wide metaplots generated ±10 kb from condensin-bound L-CID boundaries show that inter-nucleosomal contacts in log cells occur at much lower distance than in quiescent cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by metaplot analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: The distribution of inter-nucleosomal contacts dramatically shifts between log and quiescence, from transient, neighboring interactions in log to more stable, longer-range interactions in quiescence.
source: These data show that the distribution of inter-nucleosomal contacts dramatically shifts between log and quiescence, from transient, neighboring interactions in log to more stable, longer-range interactions in quiescence that are not consistent with a homogeneous zig-zag conformation.
evidence: Summary of Micro-C XL data analysis

claim: Quiescent cell chromatin fiber interactions are not consistent with a homogeneous zig-zag conformation.
source: These data show that the distribution of inter-nucleosomal contacts dramatically shifts between log and quiescence, from transient, neighboring interactions in log to more stable, longer-range interactions in quiescence that are not consistent with a homogeneous zig-zag conformation.
evidence: Inference based on contact probability patterns showing higher n+1 and n+3 interactions than expected for zig-zag

claim: Quiescent cell chromatin fibers appear more compact qualitatively compared to log cells.
source: Our results are consistent with chromatin fiber compaction in quiescent versus log cells, with quiescent cell fibers appearing more compact qualitatively and demonstrating an upward shift in diameter as compared to log even at the level of individual chromatin fibers (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by HAADF-STEM tomography imaging

claim: Quiescent cell chromatin fibers demonstrate an upward shift in diameter compared to log cells at the level of individual chromatin fibers.
source: Our results are consistent with chromatin fiber compaction in quiescent versus log cells, with quiescent cell fibers appearing more compact qualitatively and demonstrating an upward shift in diameter as compared to log even at the level of individual chromatin fibers (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by HAADF-STEM tomography imaging and surface thickness analysis

claim: Quiescent cell chromatin fibers were not as compact or as regular as fibers in chicken erythrocyte nuclei.
source: However, quiescent cell fibers were not as compact or as regular as fibers in chicken erythrocyte nuclei (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Comparison with positive control (chicken erythrocyte nuclei) shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: The average diameter of chromatin fibers in log cells is 15% less than the average chromatin fiber diameter in quiescent cells.
source: This found that the average diameter of chromatin fibers in log cell is 15% less than the average chromatin fiber diameter in Q cells, consistent with surface-thickness estimates.
evidence: Quantitative measurement using morphological erosion analysis

claim: Chromatin fibers adopt a compact and heterogeneous folded structure in quiescent cells.
source: These data are consistent with the Micro-C results and demonstrate that chromatin fibers adopt a compact and heterogeneous folded structure in quiescent cells.
evidence: Conclusion based on STEM tomography and morphological erosion analysis

claim: Modeling revealed the same 40 kb region to be more compact in quiescent compared to log cells, with the radius of gyration decreasing and nucleosome packing increasing proportionally.
source: Modeling revealed the same 40 kb region to be more compact in quiescent compared to log cells, with the radius of gyration decreasing and nucleosome packing increasing proportionally (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by mesoscale chromatin modeling simulations

claim: The modeled contact probability predicted increased n+1 contacts in log cells and a shift toward longer-range n+2 to n+6 inter-nucleosomal interactions in quiescent cells.
source: The modeled contact probability also predicted increased n+1 contacts in log cells and a shift toward longer-range n+2 to n+6 inter-nucleosomal interactions in quiescent cells, though more modest than in experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Supported by mesoscale modeling predictions

claim: Measurements were more variable for simulations of the fiber in log, consistent with a more dynamic chromatin fiber in log versus quiescent cells.
source: Measurements were also more variable for simulations of the fiber in log, consistent with a more dynamic chromatin fiber in log versus quiescent cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by variability in modeling measurements

claim: H3 and H4 tails demonstrated a striking increase in interactions with the cores of other nucleosomes in quiescence compared to log.
source: H3 and H4 tails demonstrated a striking increase in interactions with the cores of other nucleosomes in quiescence compared to log (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by mesoscale modeling measurements of tail-core contacts

claim: Quiescent and log cells have fundamentally distinct local chromatin fiber folding.
source: These results indicate that quiescent and log cells have fundamentally distinct local chromatin fiber folding.
evidence: Conclusion based on modeling results showing different interaction patterns

claim: A major difference between log and quiescent chromatin is the massive deacetylation of residues in the histone H3 and H4 tails by the histone deacetylase complex Rpd3.
source: First, a major difference between log and quiescent chromatin is the massive deacetylation of residues in the histone H3 and H4 tails by the histone deacetylase complex Rpd3 (McKnight et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (McKnight et al., 2015)

claim: TSA treatment of quiescent cells led to an increase in H4 tail acetylation approaching log cell levels as measured by ChIP-seq.
source: TSA treatment of quiescent cells led to an increase in H4 tail acetylation approaching log cell levels as measured by ChIP-seq (Figure 3A), and higher levels than log in bulk as measured by Western blot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by H4 tail penta-acetylation ChIP-seq and Western blot data

claim: TSA treatment of quiescent cells led to higher H4 tail acetylation levels than log in bulk as measured by Western blot.
source: TSA treatment of quiescent cells led to an increase in H4 tail acetylation approaching log cell levels as measured by ChIP-seq (Figure 3A), and higher levels than log in bulk as measured by Western blot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data

claim: The global lack of histone acetylation during quiescence results from ongoing deacetylation.
source: The ability to restore histone acetylation to log-equivalent levels in quiescent cells by TSA treatment implies that histone acetyltransferases are present and active in the quiescent cell nucleus, and that the global lack of histone acetylation during quiescence results from ongoing deacetylation, just as has been observed in quiescent mammalian B cells (Kieffer-Kwon et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on TSA treatment results and comparison to mammalian B cells

claim: TSA treatment significantly increased the chromatin volume of quiescent cells.
source: TSA treatment significantly increased the chromatin volume of quiescent cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and confocal imaging measurements

claim: TSA treatment reduces long-range (beyond n+3) and increases short-range (n+1 and n+2) nucleosome contacts in quiescent cells.
source: Micro-C XL data at 200 bp resolution show that TSA treatment reduces long-range (beyond n+3) and increases short-range (n+1 and n+2) nucleosome contacts (Figure 3C–D; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D for examples at lower resolution).
evidence: Supported by Micro-C XL data analysis

claim: Global histone deacetylation is required for quiescence-specific local chromatin fiber folding.
source: These results support our model that global histone deacetylation is required for quiescence-specific local chromatin fiber folding, and provide an explanation for why fiber folding is distinct in log and quiescence.
evidence: Conclusion based on TSA treatment effects on chromatin structure

claim: Alanine and glutamine substitutions of K16 (K16A and K16Q) significantly increase quiescent cell chromatin volume to a similar extent.
source: DAPI staining and volume measurements of quiescent cells show that alanine and glutamine substitutions of K16 (K16A and K16Q) significantly increase quiescent cell chromatin volume to a similar extent (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and chromatin volume measurements

claim: Substitution of both arginine residues with alanine (R17R19A) decompacts chromatin even further than K16 substitutions.
source: Substitution of both arginine residues with alanine (R17R19A) decompacts chromatin even further, and full abrogation of all five basic patch residues (16KRHRK20) with alanine (5toA) decompacts chromatin almost to G1 levels.
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and chromatin volume measurements shown in Figure 4A

claim: Full abrogation of all five basic patch residues (16KRHRK20) with alanine (5toA) decompacts chromatin almost to G1 levels.
source: Substitution of both arginine residues with alanine (R17R19A) decompacts chromatin even further, and full abrogation of all five basic patch residues (16KRHRK20) with alanine (5toA) decompacts chromatin almost to G1 levels.
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and chromatin volume measurements shown in Figure 4A

claim: During G1, neither R17R19A nor 5toA strains displayed decompaction compared to HHF2.
source: In contrast, during G1, neither R17R19A nor 5toA strains displayed decompaction compared to HHF2 (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and chromatin volume measurements in G1 cells

claim: Both R17R19A and 5toA basic patch mutants displayed strong chromatin fiber decompaction at the local level in quiescent cells.
source: In contrast, both basic patch mutants displayed strong chromatin fiber decompaction at the local level in quiescent cells (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by Micro-C XL data

claim: The pattern of local inter-nucleosomal interactions dramatically shifted in H4 basic patch mutants, with long-range interactions beyond n+2 strongly decreasing and short-range n+1 interactions increasing relative to n+2.
source: However, consistent with massive chromatin unfolding, the pattern of local inter-nucleosomal interactions dramatically shifted, with long-range interactions beyond n+2 strongly decreasing in both mutants, and short-range n+1 interactions increasing relative to n+2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by contact probability analysis from Micro-C XL data

claim: Local chromatin fiber folding in quiescent cells is mediated by inter-nucleosomal interactions driven by the H4 basic patch.
source: Collectively, these experiments support a model in which local chromatin fiber folding in quiescent cells is mediated by inter-nucleosomal interactions driven by the H4 basic patch.
evidence: Conclusion based on H4 mutant experiments showing decompaction

claim: Pol II occupancy increased dramatically in quiescent basic patch mutant cells, with occupancy increasing proportionally to the number of substitutions introduced to the basic patch.
source: In contrast, Pol II occupancy increased dramatically in quiescent basic patch mutant cells, with occupancy increasing proportionally to the number of substitutions introduced to the basic patch (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: Supported by Rpb3 ChIP-seq data

claim: The number of Pol II peaks in the 5toA mutant increased corresponding to approximately 40% of all genes.
source: ChIP-seq peak calling implemented using MACS2 similarly showed a dramatic increase in Pol II peaks between HHF2 and 5toA quiescent cells, with the number of peaks increasing in the 5toA mutant corresponding to approximately 40% of all genes (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by MACS2 peak calling analysis

claim: Fiber unfolding occurs in the basic patch mutants genome-wide, regardless of the transcriptional state of the underlying gene.
source: However, activation appears to be downstream of chromatin decompaction, as fiber unfolding occurs in the basic patch mutants genome-wide, regardless of the transcriptional state of the underlying gene (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: Supported by overlay of Pol II ChIP-seq and Micro-C XL data

claim: Local chromatin folding represses transcription, but unfolding is not sufficient for activation.
source: This suggests that local chromatin folding represses transcription, but unfolding is not sufficient for activation.
evidence: Inference based on observation that decompaction occurs genome-wide but activation is gene-specific

claim: Phenanthroline treatment leads to complete loss of Pol II occupancy by ChIP-seq.
source: Phenanthroline treatment leads to complete loss of Pol II occupancy by ChIP-seq (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by Rpb3 ChIP-seq data with phenanthroline treatment

claim: DAPI staining of phenanthroline-treated 5toA quiescent cells shows no change in chromatin volume.
source: However, DAPI staining of phenanthroline-treated 5toA quiescent cells shows no change in chromatin volume (Figure 5G, Supplementary file 1), supporting that chromatin decompaction in 5toA cells is a cause and not a result of global transcriptional activation.
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and chromatin volume measurements

claim: Chromatin decompaction in 5toA cells is a cause and not a result of global transcriptional activation.
source: However, DAPI staining of phenanthroline-treated 5toA quiescent cells shows no change in chromatin volume (Figure 5G, Supplementary file 1), supporting that chromatin decompaction in 5toA cells is a cause and not a result of global transcriptional activation.
evidence: Inference based on phenanthroline treatment experiment showing decompaction persists without transcription

claim: Stripes overlapped with condensin subunit Brn1 ChIP-seq peaks in WT quiescent cells.
source: By overlaying the ChIP-seq and Micro-C data, we identified the striking appearance of stripes that overlapped with condensin subunit Brn1 ChIP-seq peaks in WT quiescent cells (Figures 6A and 2G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by overlay of Brn1 ChIP-seq and Micro-C XL data

claim: Stripes are believed to occur in Hi-C data as a result of loop extrusion, in which SMC complexes bind the genome at two points and increase the size of the resulting loop by moving chromatin in one or both directions through the SMC ring.
source: Stripes are believed to occur in Hi-C data as a result of loop extrusion, in which SMC complexes bind the genome at two points and increase the size of the resulting loop by moving chromatin in one or both directions through the SMC ring (Goloborodko et al., 2016; Vian et al., 2018; Banigan et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on loop extrusion

claim: Aggregate peak metaplots generated from WT, R17R19A, and 5toA Micro-C data showing trans interactions between Brn1 peaks show clear stripe patterns at the mean and median in the mutants.
source: Although stripes are not observable at all Brn1 sites, aggregate peak metaplots generated from WT, R17R19A, and 5toA Micro-C data showing trans interactions between Brn1 peaks show clear stripe patterns at the mean and median in the mutants (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by aggregate peak analysis of Micro-C XL data

claim: Substitutions in the H4 tail affect the way in which condensin extrudes chromatin loops.
source: Consequently, our Micro-C results suggest that substitutions in the H4 tail affect the way in which condensin extrudes chromatin loops.
evidence: Inference based on appearance of stripes in H4 mutants but not WT

claim: Basic patch mutants show a reduction in the magnitude of Brn1 peaks and a corresponding spreading out across gene bodies on either side of promoters.
source: While Brn1 shows strong localization just upstream of transcription start sites in WT and HHF2 quiescent cells, basic patch mutants show a reduction in the magnitude of Brn1 peaks and a corresponding spreading out across gene bodies on either side of promoters (Figure 6D) and L-CID boundaries (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by Brn1 ChIP-seq data analysis

claim: MACS peak calling showed a decrease in the number of Brn1 peaks between HHF2 and 5toA.
source: MACS peak calling further showed a decrease in the number of Brn1 peaks between HHF2 and 5toA (Figure 6F), which we interpret to mean that Brn1 spreading across the genome reduces many discrete peaks to below detectable levels.
evidence: Supported by MACS2 peak calling analysis

claim: Stripes at least in part result from progressive Brn1 binding to regions of chromatin within L-CIDs, as would be expected from active loop extrusion.
source: This shows that stripes at least in part result from progressive Brn1 binding to regions of chromatin within L-CIDs, as would be expected from active loop extrusion.
evidence: Inference based on overlay of Brn1 ChIP-seq and Micro-C XL data showing correlation

claim: The emergence of stripes in Hi-C data is likely to result from an increase in the rate at which SMC complexes extrude chromatin loops.
source: Modeling studies have predicted that the emergence of stripes in Hi-C data is likely to result from an increase in the rate at which SMC complexes extrude chromatin loops: as loop extrusion occurs more rapidly, interacting regions of chromatin have less time to diffuse apart and consequently retain 'memory' of being extruded (Nuebler et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to modeling studies

claim: The change in condensin extrusion in the H4 mutants is not due to the increase in transcription in the mutants.
source: Although transcription has been proposed to affect loop extrusion through multiple avenues—by slowing the process of extrusion by creating difficult-to-traverse transcription bubbles, by 'pushing' SMC complexes across chromatin, and by promoting SMC complex loading—our data do not support that the change in condensin extrusion we see in the H4 mutants is due to the increase in transcription in the mutants (Lengronne et al., 2004; Busslinger et al., 2017; Tran et al., 2017; Zhang, 2020).
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence showing stripes occur independently of transcription

claim: Stripes occur uniformly between L-CID boundaries, regardless of Pol II occupancy.
source: This is because: (1) stripes occur uniformly between L-CID boundaries, regardless of Pol II occupancy (as seen in Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C); (2) stripes appear as strong in the R17R19A mutant as in the 5toA mutant, despite less Pol II occupancy overall; and (3) regions displaying stripes do not exhibit large changes in Pol II occupancy between WT and the mutants, because Brn1 sites tend to overlap with Pol II-occupied genes even in WT (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G; Swygert et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by comparison of Brn1 and Pol II ChIP-seq data

claim: H4 tail-mediated chromatin fiber folding sterically impedes the ability of condensin to extrude chromatin, leading to slower loop extrusion than in mutants with decompacted fibers.
source: Instead, we propose a model in which H4 tail-mediated chromatin fiber folding sterically impedes the ability of condensin to extrude chromatin, leading to slower loop extrusion than in mutants with decompacted fibers (Figure 6G).
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental observations

claim: Slower loop extrusion may help to stabilize loops between L-CID boundaries in WT quiescent cells.
source: This slower extrusion may help to stabilize loops between L-CID boundaries in WT quiescent cells.
evidence: Speculation based on proposed model

claim: Condensin depletion during quiescence entry de-represses about 20% of all genes, with genes within 1 kb of a condensin binding site disproportionately represented.
source: We previously found that condensin depletion during quiescence entry de-represses about 20% of all genes, with genes within 1 kb of a condensin binding site disproportionately represented (Swygert et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: There are nearly double the number of distinct Pol II peaks in the 5toA mutant compared to SMC4-off cells.
source: While many Pol II peaks appear in both SMC4-off and 5toA cells, there are large numbers of non-overlapping Pol II peaks, with nearly double the number of distinct peaks in the 5toA mutant (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by MACS2 differential peak calling analysis

claim: Genes with the highest Pol II occupancy in SMC4-off cells tend to be close to Brn1 sites, while Pol II occupancy in 5toA cells does not necessarily overlap with Brn1.
source: As previously shown (Swygert et al., 2019), genes with the highest Pol II occupancy in SMC4-off cells tend to be close to Brn1 sites, while Pol II occupancy in 5toA cells does not necessarily overlap with Brn1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by heatmap analysis of Brn1 and Pol II ChIP-seq data

claim: The H4 mutants display significantly more fiber decompaction than SMC4-off cells, while retaining some insulation at boundaries.
source: Additionally, although condensin depletion appears to disrupt repression by decreasing insulation at L-CID boundaries and decreasing local inter-nucleosomal interactions to some extent compared to WT (Swygert et al., 2019), the H4 mutants display significantly more fiber decompaction than SMC4-off cells, while retaining some insulation at boundaries (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by Micro-C XL metaplot analysis

claim: Condensin affects local contacts differently and to a lesser extent than the H4 tail.
source: Interestingly, although short-range n+1 and n+2 nucleosome contacts increase in SMC4-off cells compared to WT, long-range (500–1000 bp) contacts do not decrease as dramatically as in the H4 mutants, resulting in similar long/short contact odds ratios (Figure 7D). These data suggest that condensin affects local contacts differently and to a lesser extent than the H4 tail, and that the inhibition of condensin loop extrusion is a complementary rather than primary mechanism of transcriptional repression by H4 tail-mediated chromatin fiber compaction.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of contact probability patterns

claim: The inhibition of condensin loop extrusion is a complementary rather than primary mechanism of transcriptional repression by H4 tail-mediated chromatin fiber compaction.
source: These data suggest that condensin affects local contacts differently and to a lesser extent than the H4 tail, and that the inhibition of condensin loop extrusion is a complementary rather than primary mechanism of transcriptional repression by H4 tail-mediated chromatin fiber compaction.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of SMC4-off and H4 mutant effects

claim: Condensin is largely responsible for regulating the transcription of genes located around condensin binding sites at L-CID boundaries during quiescence.
source: Further, while condensin is largely responsible for regulating the transcription of genes located around condensin binding sites at L-CID boundaries during quiescence, H4-mediated chromatin compaction regulates genes across the genome.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of gene expression patterns in SMC4-off and H4 mutants

claim: H4-mediated chromatin compaction regulates genes across the genome.
source: Further, while condensin is largely responsible for regulating the transcription of genes located around condensin binding sites at L-CID boundaries during quiescence, H4-mediated chromatin compaction regulates genes across the genome.
evidence: Inference based on genome-wide effects of H4 mutations on transcription

claim: Between log and quiescence, an increase in the range of local inter-nucleosomal interactions compacts chromatin fibers genome-wide.
source: Our data show that between log and quiescence, an increase in the range of local inter-nucleosomal interactions compacts chromatin fibers genome-wide.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on Micro-C and STEM data

claim: Quiescent cell fibers lack the expected increase in n+2 interactions seen in extended zig-zag 30 nm conformations by population average.
source: These fibers are less compact and entirely distinct from 30 nm fibers, as they lack the expected increase in n+2 interactions seen in extended zig-zag 30 nm conformations by population average (Micro-C), and are smaller in diameter at the individual fiber level (as determined HAADF-STEM).
evidence: Supported by Micro-C contact probability analysis

claim: Quiescent cell fibers are smaller in diameter at the individual fiber level than 30 nm fibers.
source: These fibers are less compact and entirely distinct from 30 nm fibers, as they lack the expected increase in n+2 interactions seen in extended zig-zag 30 nm conformations by population average (Micro-C), and are smaller in diameter at the individual fiber level (as determined HAADF-STEM).
evidence: Supported by HAADF-STEM measurements

claim: Quiescent cell fibers display an overall decrease in n+1 and n+2 contacts compared to cycling cells in favor of longer-range inter-nucleosomal interactions beyond 500 bp.
source: Instead, quiescent cell fibers display an overall decrease in n+1 and n+2 contacts compared to cycling cells in favor of longer-range inter-nucleosomal interactions beyond 500 bp, consistent with extensive but disordered compaction into a more heterogeneous structure.
evidence: Supported by contact probability analysis

claim: Quiescent cell fibers show extensive but disordered compaction into a more heterogeneous structure.
source: Instead, quiescent cell fibers display an overall decrease in n+1 and n+2 contacts compared to cycling cells in favor of longer-range inter-nucleosomal interactions beyond 500 bp, consistent with extensive but disordered compaction into a more heterogeneous structure.
evidence: Inference based on contact probability patterns and STEM imaging

claim: Quiescent cell fibers, like 30 nm fibers, rely on the H4 tail basic patch.
source: Despite their differences in inter-nucleosomal interaction pattern, however, quiescent cell fibers, like 30 nm fibers, rely on the H4 tail basic patch, suggesting that disordered structures in quiescent cells and compacted ordered reconstituted structures rely on a shared mechanism.
evidence: Supported by H4 mutant experiments showing decompaction

claim: Disordered structures in quiescent cells and compacted ordered reconstituted structures rely on a shared mechanism.
source: Despite their differences in inter-nucleosomal interaction pattern, however, quiescent cell fibers, like 30 nm fibers, rely on the H4 tail basic patch, suggesting that disordered structures in quiescent cells and compacted ordered reconstituted structures rely on a shared mechanism.
evidence: Inference based on shared dependence on H4 basic patch

claim: Extended chromatin fibers in log cells and compacted fibers in quiescent cells represent physiological versions of distinct fiber folding states.
source: We propose that although physiological fibers lack regular structure, most likely due to chromatin dynamics, the irregularity of nucleosome spacing and occupancy, and the binding of additional architectural factors (van Holde and Zlatanova, 2007), extended chromatin fibers in log cells and compacted fibers in quiescent cells represent physiological versions of distinct fiber folding states (Figure 7E).
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental observations

claim: The histone deacetylase complex Rpd3 is targeted across the genome during quiescence entry and massively deacetylates histone H3 and H4 tails.
source: We previously found that the histone deacetylase complex Rpd3 is targeted across the genome during quiescence entry and massively deacetylates histone H3 and H4 tails (McKnight et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Loss of Rpd3 leads to defects in quiescence entry and quiescent cell longevity, and prevents global transcriptional repression.
source: Loss of Rpd3 leads to defects in quiescence entry and quiescent cell longevity, and prevents global transcriptional repression.
evidence: Supported by previous work on Rpd3 function

claim: Mammalian quiescent cells exhibit widespread histone deacetylation.
source: Similarly, mammalian quiescent cells exhibit widespread histone deacetylation (Rawlings et al., 2011; Evertts et al., 2013; Kieffer-Kwon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: There is a conserved mechanism for the role of histone deacetylases in regulating transcription during quiescence.
source: Consequently, our current results suggest a conserved mechanism for the role of histone deacetylases in regulating transcription during quiescence.
evidence: Inference based on similarities between yeast and mammalian quiescence

claim: H4K16Ac increases the most of all chromatin modifications upon B-cell activation.
source: Consistently, H4K16Ac is commonly implicated in mediating transitions in state. For example, H4K16Ac increases the most of all chromatin modifications upon B-cell activation (Kieffer-Kwon et al., 2017), bookmarks genes for expression during zygotic genome activation in flies (Samata et al., 2020), and disrupts dosage compensation (Wells et al., 2012; Copur et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: H4K16Ac bookmarks genes for expression during zygotic genome activation in flies.
source: Consistently, H4K16Ac is commonly implicated in mediating transitions in state. For example, H4K16Ac increases the most of all chromatin modifications upon B-cell activation (Kieffer-Kwon et al., 2017), bookmarks genes for expression during zygotic genome activation in flies (Samata et al., 2020), and disrupts dosage compensation (Wells et al., 2012; Copur et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: H4K16Ac disrupts dosage compensation.
source: Consistently, H4K16Ac is commonly implicated in mediating transitions in state. For example, H4K16Ac increases the most of all chromatin modifications upon B-cell activation (Kieffer-Kwon et al., 2017), bookmarks genes for expression during zygotic genome activation in flies (Samata et al., 2020), and disrupts dosage compensation (Wells et al., 2012; Copur et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Local chromatin fiber compaction mediated by the H4 basic patch drives transcriptional repression in quiescent cells.
source: Our data show that local chromatin fiber compaction mediated by the H4 basic patch drives transcriptional repression in quiescent cells.
evidence: Conclusion based on H4 mutant experiments showing increased transcription with decompaction

claim: In quiescent mammalian B cells, chromatin nanodomains mediated by inter-nucleosomal interactions do not decompact in the absence of transcriptional activation and a resulting increase in ATP production by Myc.
source: This result is in contrast to findings in quiescent mammalian B cells, in which histone acetylation by TSA treatment leads to an expansion in chromatin volume, but chromatin nanodomains mediated by inter-nucleosomal interactions do not decompact in the absence of transcriptional activation and a resulting increase in ATP production by Myc (Kieffer-Kwon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: TSA treatment does not decompact chromatin as extensively as abrogation of the basic patch.
source: Importantly, our results show that TSA treatment does not decompact chromatin as extensively as abrogation of the basic patch, so it is likely that chromatin decompaction upon quiescence exit requires pathways in addition to H4K16Ac.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of TSA and H4 mutant effects

claim: Chromatin decompaction upon quiescence exit likely requires pathways in addition to H4K16Ac.

claim: During quiescence entry, condensin forms L-CID loops by the process of extrusion.

evidence: Model proposed based on experimental observations and previous work

claim: As chromatin fibers compact, the rate of condensin extrusion decreases or stalls, resulting in persisting loops but not stripes in quiescent cells.
source: As chromatin fibers compact, the rate of extrusion decreases or stalls, resulting in persisting loops but not stripes in quiescent cells.
evidence: Model proposed based on absence of stripes in WT but presence in mutants

claim: In quiescent murine B cells, existing cohesin loops can persist for hours in the absence of ATP.
source: Support for this model comes from quiescent murine B cells, in which existing cohesin loops can persist for hours in the absence of ATP, and cohesin stripes increase on B cell activation (Vian et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Cohesin stripes increase on B cell activation.
source: Support for this model comes from quiescent murine B cells, in which existing cohesin loops can persist for hours in the absence of ATP, and cohesin stripes increase on B cell activation (Vian et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Yeast condensin has been shown to extrude loops in one direction in vitro.
source: Interestingly, although yeast condensin has been shown to extrude loops in one direction in vitro (Ganji et al., 2018), we see that stripes and condensin spreading emanate from boundaries in both directions.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Stripes and condensin spreading emanate from boundaries in both directions in yeast quiescent cells.
source: Interestingly, although yeast condensin has been shown to extrude loops in one direction in vitro (Ganji et al., 2018), we see that stripes and condensin spreading emanate from boundaries in both directions.
evidence: Supported by Micro-C and ChIP-seq data

claim: Multiple condensins bind L-CID boundaries and extrude loops in opposite directions, possibly through a version of the handcuff model in which an anti-parallel dimer of condensins is loaded at boundaries.
source: These data support a model in which multiple condensins bind L-CID boundaries and extrude loops in opposite directions, possibly through a version of the handcuff model in which an anti-parallel dimer of condensins is loaded at boundaries (Banigan and Mirny, 2020c).
evidence: Model proposed based on bi-directional stripe patterns

claim: Stripes can be observed extending across multiple L-CID boundaries in yeast just as they do in mammals.
source: Further, although the CTCF-dependent mechanism of loop domain boundary formation present in mammalian cells is not conserved in yeast, stripes can be observed extending across multiple L-CID boundaries in yeast just as they do in mammals (Vian et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by Micro-C data and comparison to mammalian cells

claim: Yeast boundaries are not always sufficient to block SMC complex extrusion, perhaps through boundary bypass or the absence of boundary elements in a subset of cells in the population.
source: This suggests that, as in mammalian cells, yeast boundaries are not always sufficient to block SMC complex extrusion, perhaps through boundary bypass or the absence of boundary elements in a subset of cells in the population.
evidence: Inference based on observation of stripes crossing boundaries

claim: Local chromatin fiber contacts can fundamentally change during physiologically relevant conditions.
source: Collectively, our data show that local chromatin fiber contacts can fundamentally change during physiologically relevant conditions, and that contacts consistent with local chromatin fiber folding can repress transcription and loop extrusion.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental data

claim: Nucleosomes are arranged on DNA into a 'beads on a string' conformation approximately 10 nanometers (nm) in diameter called the 10 nm fiber.
source: Nucleosomes are arranged on DNA into a 'beads on a string' conformation approximately 10 nanometers (nm) in diameter called the 10 nm fiber (Kornberg, 1974; Davies and Haynes, 1976; Finch and Klug, 1976).

claim: The position and occupancy of nucleosomes on the 10 nm fiber are highly regulated and contribute to transcriptional modulation by impeding transcription factor binding and retarding polymerase elongation.

claim: A longstanding hypothesis has been that an even greater level of transcriptional regulation is conferred by the arrangement of 10 nm fibers into three-dimensional higher-order chromatin structures mediated by interactions between nucleosomes located near each other on the DNA strand.
source: A longstanding hypothesis has been that an even greater level of transcriptional regulation is conferred by the arrangement of 10 nm fibers into three-dimensional higher-order chromatin structures mediated by interactions between nucleosomes located near each other on the DNA strand (Woodcock et al., 1984; Woodcock and Ghosh, 2010; Maeshima et al., 2021; Luger et al., 1997; Dorigo et al., 2004; Schalch et al., 2005).
evidence: Established hypothesis in the field supported by citations

claim: Mapping chromatin fiber structure at the local nucleosome level in cells and determining its relationship to physiological processes has been technically challenging.

claim: ChromEMT found that regardless of cell state, chromatin fibers exist in heterogeneous forms 5–24 nm in diameter.
source: This work found that regardless of cell state, chromatin fibers exist in heterogeneous forms 5–24 nm in diameter, suggesting that genome-wide changes in chromatin fiber compaction do not occur even in highly condensed mitotic chromosomes.

source: Although a genomics method called Micro-C that resolves three-dimensional chromatin structure at single-nucleosome resolution in cells found correlation between the number of inter-nucleosomal interactions within a gene and transcriptional activity in yeast, evidence suggests that changes in chromatin conformation may be a result of or entirely decoupled from transcription (Hsieh et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of Micro-C method supported by citation

source: Beyond local compaction, chromatin fibers are arranged into large-scale structures called chromatin domains, in which regions of chromatin preferentially interact within other regions in the same domain while being insulated from interactions with other domains (Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012; Rowley and Corces, 2018).

claim: Chromatin domain organization regulates transcription by promoting enhancer-promoter interactions within domains while inhibiting aberrant enhancer-promoter contacts between domains.
source: This organization regulates transcription by promoting enhancer-promoter interactions within domains while inhibiting aberrant enhancer-promoter contacts between domains (Hnisz et al., 2016a; Hnisz et al., 2016b).

claim: A specific form of domain, called a chromatin loop domain, is formed when ring-shaped structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMCs) complexes, such as cohesin or condensin, extrude loops of chromatin that in mammalian cells can be up to megabase size.
source: A specific form of domain, called a chromatin loop domain, is formed when ring-shaped structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMCs) complexes, such as cohesin or condensin, extrude loops of chromatin that in mammalian cells can be up to megabase size (Rao et al., 2017; Rowley and Corces, 2018; Banigan and Mirny, 2020a).

claim: How the chromatin fiber contributes to domain structure and whether or not these levels of chromatin architecture cooperate in transcriptional regulation is unknown.
source: Although chromatin organization is a highly active area of study, how the chromatin fiber contributes to domain structure and whether or not these levels of chromatin architecture cooperate in transcriptional regulation is unknown.

claim: Quiescence is a reversible state in which the cell exits the cell cycle in response to external cues and transitions to a long-lived and stress-resistant program.
source: Quiescence is a reversible state in which the cell exits the cell cycle in response to external cues and transitions to a long-lived and stress-resistant program (Gray et al., 2004; Coller et al., 2006; Cheung and Rando, 2013).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citations

claim: Entry and exit from quiescence are essential for diverse biological processes such as adult stem cell maintenance and lymphocyte activation.
source: Entry and exit from quiescence are essential for diverse biological processes such as adult stem cell maintenance and lymphocyte activation, and have been linked to drug resistance in pathogenic micro-organisms and cancer recurrence (Valcourt et al., 2012; Rittershaus et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2016).

source: Budding yeast cells enter into quiescence via a coordinated shift in metabolic and gene expression programs in response to glucose exhaustion, and can be purified from non-quiescent cells by density gradient (Gray et al., 2004; Allen et al., 2006; Sagot and Laporte, 2019).

claim: Quiescent budding yeast undergo dramatic chromatin reorganization and widespread transcriptional reprogramming.
source: Like their mammalian counterparts, quiescent budding yeast undergo dramatic chromatin reorganization and widespread transcriptional reprogramming (Lohr and Ide, 1979; Allen et al., 2006; Sagot and Laporte, 2019), making them an ideal model for determining the mechanisms and functions of three-dimensional chromatin structure in transcriptional regulation.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by citations
